The Long Game Appendices

Appendix B Preliminary draft

Probability Tables and Odds Charts

Exact figures for draws, flops, matchups, and frequencies.

This appendix holds the exact numbers behind the book: the chance of hitting a draw for every count of outs from 1 to 20, the pot odds and odds against that go with it, what a flop does to a hand, how common starting hands match up, how often you are dealt a pair and flop a set, and how many hands of each rank exist. Use it to look a number up. The ideas behind the numbers are in Chapter 5, Odds and Outs (outs), Chapter 14, Combinatorics (combinations), and Chapter 15, Board Texture (board texture), and the short versions to memorize are in Appendix A, Table Math Cheat Sheet.

Every number here was computed by program, not remembered. The draw rows use the formula in the first table's note, run through tools/poker.js. The flop counts, set odds, and hand-ranking counts come from a throwaway Node script that deals out every possible combination and scores it with the evaluator in tools/poker.js. The matchups are exact all-in equities from node tools/poker.js equity, counting every possible board.

Draws by outs

An out is an unseen card that completes your draw. Read the row for your count of outs. "Flop to river" assumes you see both the turn and the river. "Turn to river" is one card to come. "Flop to turn" is the chance the very next card hits. The last two columns are the rules of 4 and 2 from Chapter 6, Mental Math at the Table I: The Core Shortcuts, so you can see how far they drift.

The next table names the draws you meet most often, with an example of each and its count of outs. Each count was checked by listing every unseen card that makes the hand. A count covers the named draw only: if the example hand also holds an overcard, pairing it can add outs.

To turn a bet into the outs you need, multiply the equity you need by 46 unseen cards and round up. This table does that for a one-card draw on the turn. An example, not a real hand: at $2/$5 the pot is $100 on the turn and a player bets $50. The pot is now $150, and you call $50 to make it $200. You need 50 / 200 = 25 percent, which is 12 outs. A flush draw has 9, so on pot odds alone it is a fold unless you expect to win more on the river.

Some players think in odds against rather than percentages. This chart puts common draws in that form, so you can hold them up against the pot odds column above.

Flop frequencies

A flop is three cards from 52, so there are 22,100 of them. Before you look at your own hand, this is what the board will look like.

Now deal yourself a hand. The three tables below count every one of the 19,600 flops that can come with a given hand in your hand (50 unseen cards, choose 3).

Preflop matchups

These are all-in equities with no board yet, as a share of the pot you win (a tie counts as half). Suits matter a little, so each hand is shown with its suits. The first split chart gives eight matchups you will see again and again. The table below holds more.

For which of these hands to play and from where, see Chapter 4, Starting Hands and Appendix C, Preflop Range Charts.

Pairs and sets

There are 1,326 two-card starting hands (52 times 51 over 2). Every other count in this section divides by that.

A pocket pair becomes a set when one of the two remaining cards of its rank comes. The odds depend on how many cards you get to see, counted from the moment you are dealt the pair.

Hand-ranking counts

A five-card hand is one of 2,598,960 combinations. In hold'em you pick the best five of seven cards, so the rarer ranks show up more often than the five-card counts suggest. Both sets of counts are here. In the seven-card column each hand is counted once, under the best rank it makes.
